children: Resistance in Aedes aegypti could push Indian cities to rethink mosquito-control spending, accelerating demand for alternative chemistries, biological controls and digital surveillance

The emerging insecticide-resistance problem in Aedes aegypti could have significant implications for India’s dengue-control efforts and municipal spending. A 2026 Pune study found permethrin resistance in 6 of 9 tested localities, with corrected mosquito mortality ranging from 63 per cent in Warje to 91.6 per cent in Yerwada, while Kothrud recorded 99 per cent mortality and remained susceptible.

The detection of insecticide-resistant Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in parts of Pune could have consequences well beyond the immediate public-health challenge. If conventional chemicals become less effective, Indian municipalities may need to reconsider how they allocate resources for dengue prevention and move towards more targeted, integrated and data-driven mosquito control.

The shift could create opportunities for agrochemical and vector-control companies supplying alternative insecticides and larvicides, while also opening space for health-tech firms working on GIS mapping, mosquito surveillance and AI-supported outbreak prediction.

Researchers also detected resistance-associated mutations including S989P, V1016G, F1534C and T1520I. A 2023 review covering 43 Indian studies found widespread resistance to several insecticides, including DDT, malathion, deltamethrin, permethrin, lambda-cyhalothrin and temephos. In Delhi-NCR, one study found 76 per cent of larvae resistant to the WHO discriminating dose of temephos.

India reported 289,235 dengue cases and 485 deaths in 2023, while Maharashtra recorded 19,034 cases and 55 deaths that year; globally, WHO reported more than 14.4 million dengue cases and 11,201 deaths in 2024. The financial burden is also significant: one Indian cost analysis found that a state allocated about Rs 16.03 million specifically for dengue materials and supplies in its 2016 budget, alongside Rs 6.7 million for dengue-related vector-control activities and Rs 4.9 million in human-resource costs.

Resistance could therefore accelerate demand for alternatives such as Bti, spinosad, pyriproxyfen and novaluron, as well as newer insecticide chemistries such as isocycloseram and broflanilide. WHO is also encouraging stronger resistance surveillance, including standardised testing, molecular monitoring and national databases. At the same time, GIS mapping, mobile mosquito reporting, weather and environmental data, AI-based outbreak prediction and targeted interventions could become increasingly important.

The economic impact is likely to involve higher upfront spending on surveillance, laboratory testing, trained personnel and technology, but more targeted prevention could potentially reduce longer-term costs associated with hospitalisation, lost productivity and large dengue outbreaks.

Dr Shankar V, Internal Medicine Physician, Apollo Hospitals, Sheshadripuram, Bengaluru, said resistance does not necessarily mean municipalities should simply spend more on insecticides. “Resistance does not necessarily mean municipalities simply need to buy more insecticide. It means they need to spend more intelligently on surveillance, resistance testing, source reduction and targeted interventions because repeatedly spraying an ineffective chemical has little epidemiological or economic value.”

He added that India already has alternatives that could form part of a broader strategy. “There is already a pipeline of alternative tools pyriproxyfen, novaluron, Bti and spinosad for larval control, and newer chemistries such as isocycloseram internationally.” However, deployment would depend on regulatory approvals and evidence that the products work against locally resistant mosquito populations.
Beyond Blanket Spraying

Dr Amol Jaybhaye, Consultant Infectious Diseases, Narayana Health SRCC Children’s Hospital, Mumbai, said resistance could increase costs if cities have to expand monitoring and diversify their interventions. “If the chemicals used to control mosquitoes become less effective it could cost more to stop dengue. This might mean using sprays trying different types of chemicals checking for mosquitoes more often and focusing on specific areas.”

However, Jaybhaye stressed that higher expenditure is not inevitable. Early resistance detection, removal of breeding sites, larval control and appropriate insecticide use could help municipalities avoid spending resources on ineffective measures. The changing resistance landscape could also accelerate Integrated Vector Management, bringing together biological controls, larvicides, environmental management, source reduction, targeted spraying and surveillance.

Jaybhaye said, “When mosquitoes become resistant to chemicals it shows the need for ways that use many methods together instead of just one.” Such an approach could increase demand for biological larvicides such as Bti and spinosad, insect growth regulators including pyriproxyfen and novaluron, and technologies capable of identifying mosquito hotspots.
Data Could Guide Action

Municipal readiness, however, remains uneven. Jaybhaye noted that some cities are improving mosquito surveillance and adopting digital tools, while others continue to depend heavily on traditional methods. “To change cities need people who know what they are doing, data about mosquitoes labs to test things with digital systems that can work together and enough money.”

Dr Shankar said technology could become increasingly valuable if it connects mosquito breeding-site mapping, dengue surveillance and environmental information. “There could be greater demand for technologies that map breeding sites, track dengue cases and identify high-risk areas using weather and environmental data.”

AI could help identify locations at greater risk of outbreaks, while GIS systems could allow municipal teams to target interventions instead of relying on blanket spraying. Community reporting could further help authorities identify breeding sites and respond faster.

The economic implications could initially be significant, with municipalities potentially spending more on laboratory testing, trained personnel, surveillance and digital infrastructure. Yet both experts point to the possibility of longer-term savings if better prevention reduces infections, hospital visits, lost productivity and emergency outbreak response.

As resistance changes the effectiveness of established mosquito-control practices, India’s cities may increasingly need to treat dengue prevention as an integrated system rather than an insecticide-spraying exercise. The emerging market could consequently span chemicals, biological controls, surveillance infrastructure and predictive technologies while putting greater emphasis on using the right intervention in the right place.
